Gong Ageng見於爪哇與巴厘甘美蘭，為最大青銅鑼，也是爪哇語中唯一稱gon: The Gong Ageng is found in Javanese and Balinese gamelan. It is the largest bronze gong and the only large gong called gong in Javanese. Every set has at least one, commonly two, and older sets may have three or more. In the past gongs up to 135 cm in diameter were made; today the more common ones are about 80 cm or more, to fit the budgets of educational institutions. Because bronze is expensive, poorer regions use iron gongs or slotted gongs, and bronze-plated or laminated iron versions also appear. Its pitch determines the tuning and the name of the whole set; it has a similar role in Sundanese gamelan, and other Indonesian and Philippine cultures have comparable instruments called agung.

演奏鑼王時，以軟槌敲擊鑼面中央突出的拋光部位發聲。它在甘美蘭中標示大樂句（gon: To play the gong ageng you strike the raised, polished boss at the centre of the face with a soft mallet. In gamelan it marks the beginning and end of large phrases (gongan), and the stroke has to fit the tempo (irama) and the length of the structure (bentuk). For a beginner the point is the interval between long phrases, not continuous striking; in the larger pieces (gendhing) the gong ageng can carry this punctuation on its own.

鑼王主要出現於印尼爪哇甘美蘭合奏中，是編制內最大的青銅鑼，以軟槌敲擊。它用於標示: The gong ageng appears mainly in Javanese gamelan in Indonesia, where it is the largest bronze gong in the ensemble and is struck with a soft mallet. It marks large phrases, and in the larger gendhing pieces it is often used alone. The same role appears in Sundanese gamelan, for example in the degung ensemble. Balinese gamelan has smaller gongs of similar function rather than a direct equivalent of the gong ageng. It is also struck at important ceremonies, on the arrival of guests of honour and on public occasions.
鑼王的發聲體主要為青銅，是爪哇與巴里甘美蘭中最大的青銅鑼，通常以純鑄後鍛打成形，: The sounding body of the gong ageng is mainly bronze; it is the largest bronze gong in Javanese and Balinese gamelan, usually cast and then hammered into shape, and struck with a soft mallet on the raised, polished boss; the material of the soft mallet is not stated. Because bronze is costly, poorer regions and villages also have iron gong ageng or slotted substitutes, though their sound is inferior; there are also bronze-plated or bronze-laminated iron gongs.
鑼王音色低沉而有明確音高，以軟頭槌敲擊中心凸起處發聲，餘音呈多層衰減泛音，並因兩: The gong ageng's timbre is low and clearly pitched; it is struck on the central boss with a soft-headed mallet, and the sound decays in layers of overtones, with a slow beating from the slight difference between its two sides. Its fundamental can go as low as about 44.5 Hz, close to the limit of human hearing at the bottom, unlike the crash of Chinese or Turkish cymbals; smaller gongs of the same family are higher in pitch and lack the same depth.
鑼王（Gong Ageng）是印尼爪哇甘美蘭使用的體鳴樂器，為爪哇與峇里甘美蘭樂: The gong ageng is an idiophone used in Javanese gamelan in Indonesia; it is the largest bronze gong in Javanese and Balinese gamelan and the only large gong called gong in Javanese. It is a round disc narrowing at the bottom into a cone smaller than the face, with a raised, polished boss at the centre, struck with a soft mallet. In the ensemble it marks the larger phrase sections, and large pieces often use it alone; Sundanese gamelan uses it in a similar way.
